one_liner: Linux 4.14 kernel module replacing the mmap page-fault and eviction path for fast block devices; 3.7-7x more page faults/s than mmap at high thread counts.
what_it_does: FastMap is a research kernel module (dmap) that provides its own memory-mapped I/O path for a block device (/dev/dmap/dmapN) or for files under a WrapFS stacked mount (mount -t wrapfs /mnt/backing /mnt/fmap). Applications keep the plain mmap() API; any mmap of the FastMap device or of files under the wrapped mount goes through FastMap instead of the kernel page cache. Fetches and evictions use direct I/O to the underlying device or file system.
how_it_is_fast: Per the author's PhD thesis (chapter 4, based on the ATC'20 paper): it removes the centralized contention points of the Linux mmap path by keeping separate clean and dirty trees per core (radix and red-black trees, pages assigned to cores round-robin), uses full per-page reverse mappings instead of Linux object-based rmap to cut CPU work on eviction, and runs a dedicated DRAM cache with per-core free lists and clean queues plus batched TLB shootdowns. It also raises device queue depth, and adds a user-set read-ahead to pre-map pages for sequential access.
when_to_use: Research or reproduction work on mmap-heavy applications (mmap-based key-value stores such as Kreon, graph processing with Ligra, an mmap'd heap for Silo) on Optane-class NVMe where page-fault throughput, not the device, is the bottleneck.
Many threads (16-80) taking random page faults on one mapping, where Linux mmap stops scaling beyond about 8 threads on the authors' 32-core box.
Out-of-memory datasets on a fast block device where you can dedicate a fixed DRAM cache to the mapping.
A machine you can pin to Linux 4.14 (the evaluated kernel is 4.14.72) and where crashing the kernel is acceptable.
when_not_to_use: Any production system: open issue #2 (2022) reports a kernel panic on random writes (rand_threads_write) on 4.14.123 with no maintainer reply.
Modern kernels: the module resolves unexported symbols with kallsyms_lookup_name, which kernels from 5.7 on no longer export, and the README only supports 4.14.

Machines whose core count is not 32 or 80: NUM_FREELISTS is hard-coded to 32 in shared_defines.h and mmap_buffer_hash_table.c only has tables for 1, 32 or 80 (otherwise '#error NUM_FREELISTS number is not supported!'); issue #1 reports a crash on a 256-core server.
Mostly sequential workloads: the thesis reports only 6.06% average gain on MonetDB TPC-H.
If you can change the application's I/O model: io_uring or SPDK (siblings) avoid the page-fault path entirely and are maintained.

integration.dependencies: Linux 4.14 kernel source/headers; userspace ioctl tools in the repo; WrapFS (included) for the file-system mode
integration.min_toolchain: Kernel build toolchain for Linux 4.14 (compiler not documented)
integration.platforms: Linux 4.14 only; evaluated on x86-64 Intel Xeon (E5-2630 v3, E5-4610 v3)
integration.thread_safety: Designed for concurrent page faults from many threads (per-core structures); stability bugs reported (issue #2 kernel panic on writes)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — applications keep calling mmap(), but only on /dev/dmap/dmapN or files under a WrapFS mount after the module is loaded with a fixed DRAM cache size

gotchas: The README's cache-size example is wrong: perma_mmap_buf_size=1024 is 1024 4 KB pages, i.e. 4 MB, not the 4 GB it states; the default in main.c is PAGES_16G (16 GB of DRAM reserved at load).

The headline 11.8x (11.89x in the thesis) needs out-of-tree Speculative Page Fault kernel patches modified for FastMap; stock FastMap without SPF gives 4.7x (read) and 7x (write) on 80 threads, and 3.7x / 6.6x on 32 threads, all on null_blk, which discards I/O.
The 5.27x figure is Ligra BFS on a DRAM-backed pmem block device (21.9 s vs 4.15 s); on the Optane SSD the same run is 3.31x (21.3 s vs 6.42 s).
Licensing is mixed: the LICENCE file is LGPL-2.1, but main.c declares MODULE_LICENSE("GPL").
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FastMap over UMap (userfaultfd, user space) or TriCache when the application must keep using kernel mmap semantics and you can run a 4.14 kernel module; pick vmcache/exmap, UMap, liburing or SPDK for anything maintained or on a current kernel.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run measurements (ATC'20 paper, restated in Papagiannis's PhD thesis) on Linux 4.14.72, CentOS 7.3, 2x Xeon E5-2630 v3 (32 hyper-threads) and 4x Xeon E5-4610 v3 (80 hyper-threads), 256 GB DDR4, Intel Optane P4800X, null_blk and pmem: random page-fault IOPS 3.7x/6.6x (read/write) over Linux mmap at 32 threads and 4.7x/7x at 80 threads; 11.89x read IOPS only with SPF patches; Ligra BFS 3.31x on Optane, 5.27x on pmem; Kreon YCSB about 2x on average; MonetDB TPC-H +6.06%. Compiler and flags not stated; the random page-fault microbenchmarks (tests/rand_threads_read.c, tests/rand_threads_write.c) are in the repo.
status_note: Research prototype, stale since 2021-09-29 with two unanswered crash/scalability issues; LGPL-2.1 code is copyable, but it is tied to Linux 4.14 and is useful mainly as a design reference.
